text: It was once believed. <break time="0.8s" /> That development was either continuous or discontinuous. <break time="0.8s" /> But not both. <break time="0.8s" /> Today, scientists agree. <break time="0.8s" /> That development includes. <break time="0.8s" /> Both continuity and discontinuity. <break time="0.8s" /> Whether a particular developmental change appears continuous or discontinuous. <break time="0.8s" /> Depends in part. <break time="0.8s" /> On our point of view. <break time="0.8s" /> Consider physical growth. <break time="0.8s" /> We often think of increases in height. <break time="0.8s" /> As involving a slow and steady process. <break time="0.8s" /> Each month an infant is taller than the prior month. <break time="0.8s" /> Illustrating continuous change. <break time="0.8s" /> However when researchers measured infants height every day. <break time="0.8s" /> They discovered. <break time="0.8s" /> That infants have growth days and nongrowth days. <break time="0.8s" /> Days in which they show rapid change in height. <break time="0.8s" /> Mixed in with days in which there is no change in height. <break time="0.8s" /> Illustrating discontinuous change. <break time="0.8s" /> In this example. <break time="0.8s" /> Monthly measurements of infant height suggest gradual increases. <break time="0.8s" /> But daily measurements show spurts of growth. <break time="0.8s" /> Each lasting 24 hours or less. <break time="0.8s" /> Thus whether a given phenomenon, such as height. <break time="0.8s" /> Is described as continuous or discontinuous. <break time="0.8s" /> Can vary depending on the perspective. <break time="0.8s" /> Most developmental scientists agree. <break time="0.8s" /> That some aspects of development. <break time="0.8s" /> Are best described as continuous. <break time="0.8s" /> And others as discontinuous.
